title: Which is dearer?
hook: fame or your life, which is dearer? know contentment and avoid disgrace (Tao Te Ching 44)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the softest thing: chapter forty-three says the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest, and gets in where there's no crack. Your line was the softest. Where did you try a soft thing instead of a push? Day one thousand one hundred six.

Late at night, a phone lights up a face in a dark room. Refresh. How many people saw the post? Refresh. Did anyone new follow? Refresh. An hour goes by that could have been sleep, or a talk with someone in the next room, or nothing at all. Nobody chose to trade the hour. It just went. Chapter forty-four of the Tao Te Ching doesn't scold anyone for this. It asks a question instead, and leaves it standing there.
screen: `A PHONE AT MIDNIGHT.` → `REFRESH, REFRESH.` → `AN HOUR, TRADED.`

segments.voice: First, the question. James Legge set chapter forty-four in rhyme, and it opens: "Or fame or life, Which do you hold more dear? Or life or wealth, To which would you adhere?" Two questions, and the chapter doesn't answer them for you. Second, the trade. The chapter goes on to say that great attachment brings great cost, and that piling things up leads to heavy loss. It isn't saying a name or money is evil. It's pointing at the trade underneath: what you spend of your actual life to get them. Third, the way out it offers. Whoever knows contentment avoids disgrace. Whoever knows when to stop avoids danger, and can last a long time. Contentment and knowing when to stop are not prizes at the end. They're the brakes on the trade. Fourth, fame at a small scale. Fame doesn't have to mean being famous. It can be a few more likes, the boss's notice, being the one who always says yes. Each of those costs something: an evening, an hour of sleep, a weekend with someone you love. Chapter forty-four's question is a good one to carry into those moments. Not as a rule. As a weighing. Which is dearer? And this is the end of a week, so here is what it gathered: virtue without trying, rooted low, returning, they laugh, carry both, the softest, and today, which is dearer. A week of small, quiet strengths that can look like weakness from outside.
screen: `OR FAME OR LIFE?` · `WHAT YOU SPEND TO GET IT.` · `KNOW WHEN TO STOP.` · `A WEEK OF QUIET STRENGTHS.` · then, large: `WHICH IS DEARER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your life over one bit of fame. Settle and breathe. Let one small chase come to mind, something you do to be seen, praised or counted. Hold it in one hand. In the other, hold what it costs: sleep, time with someone, quiet, your attention. Don't decide yet. Just feel the weight in each hand. Then, if you're ready, set one bit of the chase down for today. The bell holds the time.
Which is dearer? Chapter forty-four's question: fame or your life, wealth or your life. Whoever knows contentment avoids disgrace. Today's word.
Your line: which is dearer. Before one check of the numbers today, likes, views, the inbox, ask the question, and see what you choose. Day one thousand one hundred six.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often use chapter forty-four's question, fame or life, as a check on chasing recognition or money at the cost of health, rest and the people around them.
